samples.summary: The guard→strategy state hand-off (`req.__oauthState` → `opts.state`) is renamed in this diff and has no test at all
samples.evidence: `github.strategy.ts` was changed from reading `__cliStateToken` to `__oauthState` and forwarding it as `opts.state` — the single wire that actually gets the CSRF-binding `state` to GitHub (the guard's own comment says "a typo in it would silently drop the binding"). `github.strategy.spec.ts` only asserts endpoint URLs (lines 33-119); it never constructs a request with `__oauthState` and never observes what is passed to `super.authenticate`. `github-auth.guard.spec.ts` asserts only that the guard *sets* `req.__oauthState`; nothing on either side proves the two names agree or that the state is forwarded. A mismatch would leave every web login unbound-or-broken with a fully green suite.

samples.summary: The web-state comparison is only tested with different-length values, so the actual constant-time comparison branch is never exercised
samples.evidence: `timingSafeEqualString` short-circuits on `left.length === right.length` before calling `timingSafeEqual`. The mismatch fixtures are `'mine'` (4 chars) vs `'theirs'` (6 chars) and `{}` vs `'theirs'` — every rejecting case is decided by the length check alone. The real attack shape is an attacker-supplied `state` of the *same* length as the victim's cookie (both are 43-char base64url values from `randomBytes(32)`), and no test covers it: an implementation that returned `true` for equal-length differing values would still pass this suite.

Grepping `packages` for `INVALID_PROXY` finds only the source file — image-fetcher.test.ts exercises a working proxy, `no_proxy`, and the warning, but never a malformed `http_proxy` value, so neither the classification nor the redaction of the proxy URL in that message is covered.

samples.summary: Export tests titled 'without writing the file' assert only the exit code

No fs spy or `existsSync` check backs the 'without writing the file' half of the claim, so a regression that wrote a partial/empty file before exiting would pass.

finding.evidence: `github.strategy.ts` was changed from reading `__cliStateToken` to `__oauthState` and forwarding it as `opts.state` — the single wire that actually gets the CSRF-binding `state` to GitHub (the guard's own comment says "a typo in it would silently drop the binding"). `github.strategy.spec.ts` only asserts endpoint URLs (lines 33-119); it never constructs a request with `__oauthState` and never observes what is passed to `super.authenticate`. `github-auth.guard.spec.ts` asserts only that the guard *sets* `req.__oauthState`; nothing on either side proves the two names agree or that the state is forwarded. verdict.reason: The guard→strategy state hand-off has no test anywhere in the repo. github.strategy.ts:59-66 reads `req.__oauthState` and forwards it as `opts.state` to `super.authenticate` — the only assignment of `opts.state` in the auth dir. github.strategy.spec.ts (read in full) constructs strategies only to read `_oauth2._authorizeUrl`/`_accessTokenUrl`/`_userProfileURL`/`_userEmailURL`; it never builds a request, never calls `authenticate`, and never observes `state`. github-auth.guard.spec.ts asserts only the producer side (`req.__oauthState` set, cookie mirrored) and stubs the parent `canActivate` (lines 38-45) so it never reaches the strategy. The two sides use independent inline structural types (`Request & { __oauthState?: string }` in the guard, `{ __oauthState?: string }` in the strategy) with no shared constant or interface, so a rename drift is not caught by the compiler either. I searched wide for a counterexample and found none: repo-wide grep for `__oauthState`/`oauthState`/`cliStateToken` hits only those three files; no test anywhere spies on `Strategy.prototype`/`passport-oauth2`/`passport-github2`; no e2e spec in packages/backend/test hits `/auth/github` or inspects a redirect Location for `state=` (the only github/oauth mentions are env stubs at test/helpers/integration-helpers.ts:88-95); auth.controller.spec.ts covers only the inbound callback verification (lines 244-282); packages/cli/test/login.test.ts:346 asserts the CLI's own URL construction. A name mismatch would silently drop the CSRF binding on every web login with a fully green suite — a clear behavior change with no meaningful test, major under the missing-tests lane.

verdict.reason: Verified in the repo: `timingSafeEqualString` (auth.controller.ts:39-43) short-circuits on `left.length === right.length` before `timingSafeEqual`, and `consumeWebOAuthState` (auth.controller.ts:255-266) rejects earlier on `!stateToken` and `typeof cookie !== 'string'`. Every rejection fixture in auth.controller.spec.ts:265-268 is decided by one of those pre-checks: 'mine'(4) vs 'theirs'(6) is a length mismatch, `{}` vs 'theirs' hits the non-string-cookie guard, and 'mine' vs undefined hits the missing-state guard. The only equal-length case is the happy path (auth.controller.spec.ts:251-254, 'web-state' vs 'web-state'). Consequently an implementation that returned true for equal-length but differing values (i.e. dropping `timingSafeEqual` entirely) passes the whole suite, so the actual attack shape — an attacker-supplied state of the same length as the victim's 43-char cookie — is untested. I searched beyond the reviewer's stated ground: github-auth.guard.spec.ts (only mints/mirrors the state cookie, lines 128-172, never exercises the callback comparison), all packages/backend/test/*.e2e-spec.ts (no auth/github/callback exercise; integration-helpers.ts:94 only configures the URL), and repo-wide greps for githubAuthCallback / consumeWebOAuthState / web-state / timingSafeEqualString, which surface only these two auth files (other hits are vendored node_modules). No counterexample exists.
